scenario: A client is being discharged after a posterior-approach total hip arthroplasty.
questionText: Which statements by the client indicate understanding of hip precautions? Select all that apply.

options.text: "I will use a raised toilet seat."
"I will keep a pillow between my knees when I lie on my side."
"I can cross my legs when I sit if it is comfortable."
"I will use a long-handled reacher to pick things up from the floor."
"I will sit in a low, soft armchair so I can relax."

rationale: After a posterior approach, flexing the hip beyond 90°, adducting it past the midline and internally rotating it increase the risk of dislocation. A raised toilet seat, an abduction pillow between the knees and a reacher help avoid these positions. Crossing the legs causes adduction, and low soft chairs cause excessive hip flexion.
references: Total hip arthroplasty postoperative care — standard orthopaedic nursing content
reviewNotes: Hip precautions vary by surgeon and approach; keyed for a posterior approach as stated in the stem.

scenario: An 82-year-old client with mild cognitive impairment is admitted with a urinary tract infection and has a high fall-risk score.
questionText: Which interventions should the nurse implement? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep the bed in the lowest position with the brakes locked.
Offer toileting assistance on a regular schedule.
Raise all four side rails at night.
Place the call light and personal items within reach.
Apply a vest restraint while the client is in bed.

rationale: A low, locked bed, scheduled toileting (a UTI increases urgency), items within reach and non-slip footwear are evidence-based fall-prevention measures. Four raised side rails are considered a restraint and increase injury when confused clients climb over them. A vest restraint is not a fall-prevention intervention and requires a prescription and least-restrictive justification.
references: AHRQ Preventing Falls in Hospitals toolkit

questionText: The nurse is reviewing assessment findings for clients with heart failure. For each finding, specify whether it is associated with left-sided heart failure, right-sided heart failure or both.
instructions: Each finding may have more than one answer.
rationale: Left-sided failure causes back-up into the pulmonary circulation, producing crackles and orthopnoea. Right-sided failure causes systemic venous congestion, producing jugular venous distension, dependent oedema and hepatomegaly. Reduced cardiac output causes fatigue in both.
references: Heart failure clinical manifestations — standard medical-surgical nursing content

questionText: For each medication, specify the laboratory value or values the nurse should monitor to evaluate safety or effectiveness.
instructions: Each medication may have more than one answer.
rationale: The INR guides warfarin dosing. The aPTT (or anti-Xa level) guides an unfractionated heparin infusion, and the platelet count screens for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. Furosemide, a loop diuretic, can cause hypokalaemia, and spironolactone, a potassium-sparing diuretic, can cause hyperkalaemia; both require potassium monitoring.
references: Anticoagulant and diuretic monitoring — standard pharmacology nursing content

questionText: For each client condition, specify the transmission-based precaution the nurse should implement in addition to standard precautions.
rationale: Tuberculosis and measles are spread by small airborne particles, which require an airborne infection isolation room and an N95 respirator. Influenza and pertussis are spread by large respiratory droplets, which require a mask within close range. MRSA in uncontained drainage and C. difficile are spread by direct and indirect contact, which requires a gown and gloves.
references: CDC 2007 Guideline for Isolation Precautions, Appendix A

scenario: The nurse is assessing a term newborn.
questionText: For each finding, specify whether it is expected or unexpected.

matrixRows.text: Bluish hands and feet at 1 hour of age
Elongated head shape after vaginal birth
Yellow skin colour at 12 hours of age

rationale:
Acrocyanosis in the first hours, a heart rate of about 110–160/min and moulding after vaginal birth are expected.

A respiratory rate above 60/min with nasal flaring indicates respiratory distress. An axillary temperature below about 36.5 °C is hypothermia. Jaundice appearing within the first 24 hours is pathological and needs evaluation.
references: Newborn assessment — standard maternal–newborn nursing content

scenario: A client is admitted with acute pancreatitis. Serum lipase is 3 times the upper limit of normal, and the client reports severe epigastric pain radiating to the back.
questionText: For each nursing intervention, specify whether it is indicated or contraindicated.

matrixRows.text: Administer IV opioid analgesia as prescribed
Maintain IV fluid therapy as prescribed
Offer a high-fat meal to stimulate appetite
Assist the client to sit up and lean forward for comfort
Allow a small amount of alcohol to prevent withdrawal

rationale:
Pain control, aggressive IV fluids (to counter fluid shifts) and an upright, forward-leaning position are core measures. Glucose is monitored because pancreatic damage can impair insulin secretion.

Fat stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion and worsens pain. Alcohol directly injures the pancreas; withdrawal is managed pharmacologically, not with alcohol.
references: Acute pancreatitis — standard medical-surgical nursing content

scenario: A client returned from cardiac catheterisation through the right femoral artery 2 hours ago.
questionText: For each finding, specify whether it is expected or unexpected.

matrixRows.text: Right pedal pulse 2+, equal to the left
Small, flat bruise around the puncture site
Firm, enlarging swelling at the puncture site
Right foot cool and pale compared with the left
New back pain with blood pressure falling from 132/80 to 98/60 mm Hg
Client reports discomfort from lying flat

rationale:
Equal distal pulses, a small flat bruise and discomfort from prescribed bed rest are expected.

An enlarging haematoma indicates bleeding at the site. A cool, pale foot suggests arterial occlusion. Back or flank pain with hypotension suggests retroperitoneal bleeding, an emergency.
references: Care after cardiac catheterisation — standard cardiovascular nursing content

scenario: A client with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and a documented history of chronic hypercapnia (baseline PaCO₂ 58 mm Hg) is admitted with an exacerbation. Oxygen is prescribed.
questionText: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
dropdownTemplate: The nurse should titrate oxygen to maintain an SpO₂ of {{target}} because excessive oxygen may cause {{risk}}.

options.text: drying of the nasal mucosa only

rationale: In clients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, a target SpO₂ of 88–92% avoids hypoxaemia while limiting oxygen-induced hypercapnia. That hypercapnia arises from worsened ventilation–perfusion matching and the Haldane effect, with a smaller contribution from reduced respiratory drive.
references: British Thoracic Society guideline for oxygen use in healthcare and emergency settings (2017)

scenario: Fifteen minutes after starting a unit of packed red blood cells, the client reports chills and low back pain. Temperature has risen from 37.0 °C (98.6 °F) to 38.6 °C (101.5 °F), heart rate 118/min and blood pressure 92/58 mm Hg (baseline 128/76 mm Hg).
questionText: Complete the table by selecting the best choice for each clinical decision.

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride through the blood tubing

dropdownFields.label: Items to send to the blood bank

options.text: Blood bag, tubing and a new blood sample

rationale: Fever, chills, flank or back pain, tachycardia and hypotension soon after starting red cells indicate an acute haemolytic reaction. The nurse stops the transfusion immediately and keeps the IV line open with 0.9% sodium chloride through new tubing, so no more donor blood enters the vein. The bag, tubing and new blood (and usually urine) samples are sent for investigation. Dextrose solutions haemolyse red cells and are never used with blood.
references: Transfusion reaction management — standard medical-surgical nursing content

scenario: On the first day after total thyroidectomy, a client reports tingling around the mouth and in the fingertips. Tapping in front of the ear produces twitching of the facial muscles.
questionText: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
dropdownTemplate: The nurse recognises that the findings suggest {{cond}} and should {{action}}.

options.text: notify the provider and prepare IV calcium gluconate
give an extra dose of levothyroxine
apply an ice pack to the neck
reassure the client that this is expected and will pass

rationale: Perioral and fingertip paraesthesias and a positive Chvostek sign indicate hypocalcaemia from parathyroid injury or removal during thyroidectomy. It can progress to tetany and laryngospasm, so the provider is notified, and IV calcium gluconate is kept ready and given as prescribed.
references: Post-thyroidectomy complications — standard medical-surgical nursing content

scenario: A client at 32 weeks' gestation telephones the prenatal clinic. The nurse documents the call.
questionText: Click to highlight the findings that require immediate follow-up.

highlightItems.text: Client reports a headache since this morning that acetaminophen has not relieved.
Client reports mild ankle swelling in the evenings.
Client reports heartburn after large meals.
Client reports pain under the ribs on the right side.
Client reports the baby is moving as usual.
Client reports her face and hands became puffy over the past 2 days.
Client reports a dull low backache when standing for long periods.

rationale:
A persistent headache unresponsive to analgesics, visual disturbances and right upper quadrant or epigastric pain are severe features of preeclampsia. New swelling of the face and hands warrants same-day blood pressure and urine protein evaluation.

Evening ankle oedema, heartburn after meals, normal fetal movement and low backache are common in the third trimester.
references: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 222: Gestational Hypertension and Preeclampsia (2020)

scenario: A client with schizophrenia started clozapine 6 weeks ago and attends a clinic visit.
questionText: Click to highlight the findings that require immediate follow-up.

highlightItems.text: Weight gain of 2 kg since starting clozapine
Drooling on the pillow at night
Resting heart rate 122/min with new chest discomfort
Drowsy for the first hour after waking

rationale:
Fever and sore throat may signal infection from clozapine-induced agranulocytosis, which requires an urgent absolute neutrophil count. Resting tachycardia with chest discomfort in the first 2 months of therapy raises concern for clozapine-induced myocarditis.

Modest weight gain, hypersalivation and morning sedation are common adverse effects that are managed but not emergencies. A bowel movement yesterday is normal.
references: Clozapine prescribing information — boxed warnings (severe neutropenia, myocarditis)

scenario: Five minutes after an IV infusion of ceftriaxone is started, a client reports throat tightness and itching. The nurse observes hives on the chest, wheezing and swelling of the lips. Blood pressure has fallen from 124/78 to 84/50 mm Hg, and heart rate is 128/min.
questionText: Complete the diagram by selecting from the choices below. Specify the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

options.text: Slow the infusion rate and reassess in 15 minutes
Give oral diphenhydramine as the first medication
Sit the client upright with legs dangling

rationale: Sudden skin and mucosal involvement with respiratory compromise and hypotension after drug exposure meets the criteria for anaphylaxis. The nurse stops the trigger and gives intramuscular epinephrine, the first-line treatment. Antihistamines are adjuncts, not first-line. A hypotensive client should lie supine with legs raised rather than sit upright. Airway, breathing and blood pressure are monitored closely, because swelling and shock can progress or recur.

scenario: A client is 1 day after abdominal surgery and has a morphine patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) pump. The client is difficult to arouse and falls asleep mid-sentence. Respirations are 7/min and shallow, SpO₂ is 86% on room air, and pupils are pinpoint.
questionText: Complete the diagram by selecting from the choices below. Specify the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

options.text: Give a PCA bolus for pain
Dim the lights and allow the client to rest
Teach the family to press the PCA button

rationale: Increasing sedation, a respiratory rate below 8/min, hypoxaemia and miosis in a client receiving opioids indicate opioid-induced respiratory depression. The nurse stops the opioid and gives naloxone, titrated as prescribed. Sedation level and respiratory rate and depth are monitored closely, because naloxone's duration may be shorter than morphine's. PCA by proxy (family pressing the button) is unsafe.
references: ASPMN guidelines on monitoring for opioid-induced advancing sedation and respiratory depression
